title: Intentions Behind a Career
summary: The foundation of a truly successful and fulfilling career in Islam begins not with a job title, salary figure, or university degree but with intention (niyyah).
bodyMd:
## Define your Intention - *Niyyah*

> “إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ، وَإِنَّمَا لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مَا نَوَى”

The foundation of a truly successful and fulfilling career in Islam begins not with a job title, salary figure, or university degree but with **intention** (*niyyah*).

- **Why are you pursuing this career? **

- **Who do you hope to serve through it? **

- **What kind of legacy are you building?**

Your intention transforms your career from a means of survival into an **act of worship**, a **form of da’wah**, and a **contribution to the Ummah**.

When you intend to serve Allah through your work, no matter the field, your career becomes infused with barakah. Whether you’re a teacher, designer, doctor, engineer, or entrepreneur, it becomes a path to earn not just a living, but *ajr* (reward), *dignity*, and *influence*.

## Why Intention Matters in Your Career

In a world obsessed with external success: job titles, followers, or financial gain, Islam centres us on what truly matters: **sincerity**.

It’s not about the *most* deeds. It’s about the *best*. And the best deeds are those done with **sincere, pure intentions**.

A career pursued with intention:

- Grounds you in an **Allah-Conscious Mindset**, even in secular spaces.

- Shields your heart from ego, greed, and burnout.

- Keeps your purpose centred around **benefiting others**, not just personal gain.

When you realign your heart, even mundane tasks gain spiritual value. The Prophet ﷺ taught us that even feeding your family or helping a stranger can be a form of charity - if done for Allah.

> ### Reminder: Strive with your wealth and your lives
> **يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلَىٰ تِجَـٰرَةٍۢ تُنجِيكُم مِّنْ عَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍۢ
> تُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَتُجَـٰهِدُونَ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ بِأَمْوَٰلِكُمْ وَأَنفُسِكُمْ ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُون
> O believers! Shall I guide you to an exchange that will save you from a painful punishment?
> ˹It is to˺ have faith in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is best for you, if only you knew. (As-Saf 61:10-11)**
> **Reciter: Al-Saut Al-Baki Al-Shaykh Muhammad Siddiq Al-Minshawi

## Three Higher Purposes of a Career in Islam

### 1. **Your Career is a Platform for Influence**

The skills and platforms you acquire through your career can be used to shape ideas, uplift people, and lead society toward better outcomes.

Muslims today should aim to be at the **forefront of every industry** - not just to succeed personally, but to **influence systems** ethically and build a more equitable society. This includes:

- Ethical tech solutions

- Honest media narratives

- Compassionate healthcare

- Equitable education

Your job is not just a place you go - it’s a stage upon which values are expressed and legacies are written.

### 2. **A Career Gives You Dignified Independence**

Islam encourages us to work, strive, and provide for our families with honour - not out of greed, but to avoid unnecessary dependence.

Work is a means of earning **halal provision** (*rizq*), caring for others, and gaining independence. The Prophet ﷺ praised those who worked with their own hands and discouraged idleness or reliance without need.

> اليد العليا خير من اليد السفلى 
The upper hand is better than the lower hand.

A career that supports your family, enables you to give in charity, and frees you from compromising your faith is *virtuous*.

### 3. **Your Career Can Build the Community**

Islam is not a private religion - it’s a civilization-building faith. From the earliest days, Muslims built institutions: **masajid, hospitals, libraries, schools**, and social infrastructure that uplifted communities.

Behind these institutions were people with **professions**: engineers, builders, traders, physicians, and administrators - all working with an aligned intention.

Today, too, we need:

- Muslim educators shaping values in classrooms

- Muslim entrepreneurs solving ethical problems

- Muslim creatives telling our stories with dignity

- Muslim scientists advancing medicine with integrity

When your intention is to serve and strengthen the community, even your career becomes an **act of leadership** and a **sadaqah jariyah** (ongoing charity).

## Anchor Your Career in Sincere Intentions

Here are a few sample intentions that can guide your career journey:

- *“I intend to earn a halal income to support my family and uplift my community.”*

- *“I intend to use my skills to serve truth, justice, and knowledge.”*

- *“I intend to pursue excellence as a Muslim role model in my field.”*

- *“I intend to challenge harmful systems and bring about ethical solutions.”*

- *“I intend to give in charity and build something lasting for the sake of Allah.”*

> ### In Closing: Let Your Intention Lead
> - Your career is not just a way to live - it’s a way to give.
> - With sincere *niyyah*, even a spreadsheet or a stethoscope becomes a form of *ibadah*.
> - With purpose and sincerity, your 9–5 becomes your path to Paradise.

Points in this page were inspired by a lecture by Ustadh Hisham Abu Yusuf, we highly recommend watching the full video when you have some time:

title: Choosing a Career Path
summary: A career isn’t just “what job you do.” It’s the long-term path of your life - your direction, your legacy, and a huge part of how you'll be judged in this world and the next.
bodyMd:
## **What is a Career?**

A career isn’t just “what job you do.” It’s the **long-term path of your life** - your direction, your legacy, and a huge part of how you'll be judged in this world and the next.

Think of it like this:

You’ll spend **30+ years of your life** working 8+ hours a day — that’s a **massive chunk of your life**. So it can’t just be about making money or pleasing your parents. Your career should:

- Use the **skills and gifts Allah gave you**.

- Be something that helps others or **brings goodness** into the world.

- Most importantly, it should be something that **pleases Allah** and passes His test.

## **The Big 3 Career Questions**

To build a purposeful career, ask yourself:

### **What are you good at?**

- What subjects, skills, or tasks come naturally to you?

- What do others compliment you for?

### **What do you enjoy doing?**

- What kind of work gives you energy instead of draining it?

### **What is needed in the world?**

- What problems need solving? What skills are in demand?

- What can help your community, or the world at large?

 Where these three things **overlap**, you’ll find your **true path** — especially when you do it **for the sake of Allah**.

Take some time to reflect and answer each of these questions. Look for patterns or similarities between each of the categories.

## **Purpose, Worship & Accountability**

> ### Reminder: Life is a test
> **ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلْمَوْتَ وَٱلْحَيَوٰةَ لِيَبْلُوَكُمْ أَيُّكُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًۭا ۚ وَهُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْغَفُورُ
> ˹He is the One˺ Who created death and life in order to test which of you is best in deeds. And He is the Almighty, All-Forgiving. Surah Mulk (67:2)**
> **Reciter: Al-Saut Al-Baki Al-Shaykh Muhammad Siddiq Al-Minshawi**

On the Day of Judgment, you’ll be asked:

- How did you earn your money?

- How did you spend your time?

A career done **with the right intention** becomes **a form of worship**. Even building houses (like a builder) becomes rewardable if:

- The work is **halal **(aligned with Islamic ethics)

- It serves others (e.g. housing families),

- It’s done with **gratitude and ihsaan (excellence)**.

You don’t have to become an imam or scholar to live purposefully. Just be **intentional** in your career — and **align it with your faith**.

## **Unreasonable Man Thinking: Break the Mould**

> “The reasonable man adapts himself to the world. The unreasonable one tries to adapt the world to himself. Therefore, all progress depends on the unreasonable man.” – George Bernard Shaw

Most people follow the system:

- Choose the “safe” job

- Follow the crowd

- Never question why

But if you want to **make a difference**, you need to be **unreasonable** in the right way:

- Ask **why** at every step.

- Don’t accept low expectations.

- Think **from first principles** (What does Allah want? What is true? What is right?).

- **Go against the grain** if it means staying true to your values.

## Traditional Career Fields: Explained with Purpose

A brief look at career routes commonly pursued by students in the UK - what they involve, how they serve society, and where they might take you.

> ### Industry specific guides coming soon…
> For more specific guidance on how to break into each field we are making guides by industry in collaboration with professionals who have been there and done that
> Join our [WhatsApp community](https://forms.gle/vqu7oRBWwtCm7G9e8) to keep up to date

## Alternative Paths

### ** Startups & Entrepreneurship**

Some graduates choose to start their own traditional business or develop a high-growth startup.

Universities, incubators, and funding programs offer support, mentoring, and resources to help turn ideas into successful ventures.

Important to note that this is arguably one of the hardest paths you can go down but for many the potential upside is worth it.

### ** Further Educational Qualifications**

Graduates may pursue further study to specialise, improve career prospects, or meet industry requirements.

Options include Master’s degrees, and PhDs, but also professional qualifications like ACA (Accounting), LPC (Law), CFA (Finance), and PGCE (Teaching).

### ** Freelancing or Gig Work**

Some graduates may choose to pursue freelancing or gig work as an alternative to traditional employment. This path involves offering services independently—such as writing, design, web development, or consulting - on a project or contract basis.

Others may engage in gig-based platforms such as Upwork to generate income while maintaining flexibility.

### ** Content Creator**

Produces videos, blogs, or podcasts on platforms like YouTube, TikTok, or Spotify. Income comes from ads, sponsors, or merchandise. Can be done part-time alongside a job or education.

### ** Non-Profits & Volunteering**

Graduates can work with charities, NGOs, or aid organisations to create social impact.

Opportunities span education, healthcare, environmental work, Islamic initiatives, and more.

Roles may be full-time or part-time, paid or unpaid depending on the type of work and organisation.

## How to make Istikharā?

Now that (hopefully) you have an idea of what you want to do, it’s important to ensure seek divine aid in making that decision.

### Stage 1: Identifying the decision

Put into words the decision you need to make. For example, “I need to decide whether or not to
pursue a career in Software Engineering”

### Stage 2: Research and Shura (consultation)

Next, consult other wise and trusted people, for example, people in those fields, family
and friends for their advice on the matter and gather all of the** pros and cons.**

### Stage 3: Analyse costs and benefits

List the the pros and cons in writing and weigh them up.

### Stage 4: Make a Preliminary Decision

A lot of people forget this, but you should have a preliminary final decision in mind before making Istikharah (e.g. “I think the best decision is going ahead with applying for chemical engineering”).

Make sure to leave emotions aside for making that preliminary final decision.

### Stage 5: Istikharah Dua

Istikhara is the process of seeking divine aid in making the right decision. All you need to do is
pray two rakaʿāt of voluntary prayer, then read the Du’a for Istikharah below.

Remember to makesure you already have an idea of the correct decision before you do this stage.

If there is no time to pray the 2 rakaʿāt (e.g. an urgent decision needs to be made), you can read the dua without the prayer.

> اَللّٰهُمَّ إِنِّيْ أَسْتَخِيْرُكَ بِعِلْمِكَ ، وَأَسْتَقْدِرُكَ بِقُدْرَتِكَ ، وَأَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ الْعَظِيْمِ ، فَإِنَّكَ تَقْدِرُ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ ، وَتَعْلَمُ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ ، وَأَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوْبِ . اَللّٰهُمَّ إِنْ كُنْتَ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ هٰذَا الْأَمْرَ (وَيُسَمِّي حَاجَتَه) خَيْرٌ لِّيْ فِيْ دِيْنِيْ وَمَعَاشِيْ وَعَاقِبَةِ أَمْرِيْ ، فَاقْدُرْهُ لِيْ وَيَسِّرْهُ لِيْ ثُمَّ بَارِكْ لِيْ فِيْهِ ، وَإِنْ كُنْتَ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ هٰذَا الْأَمْرَ (وَيُسَمِّي حَاجَتَه) شَرٌّ لِّيْ فِيْ دِيْنِيْ وَمَعَاشِيْ وَعَاقِبَةِ أَمْرِيْ ، فَاصْرِفْهُ عَنِّيْ وَاصْرِفْنِيْ عَنْهُ وَاقْدُرْ لِيَ الْخَيْرَ حَيْثُ كَانَ ثُمَّ أَرْضِنِيْ بِهِ

> Allāhumma innī astakhīruka bi ʿilmik, wa astaqdiruka bi qudratik, wa as’aluka min faḍlika-l-ʿaẓīm, fa innaka taqdiru wa lā aqdir, wa taʿlamu wa lā aʿlam, wa Anta ʿAllāmu-l-ghuyūb. Allāhumma in kunta taʿlamu an-na hādha-l-amra (mention matter in any language) khayrul-lī fī dīnī wa maʿāshī wa ʿāqibati amrī, faqdurhu lī wa yassirhu lī thumma bārik lī fīhī, wa in kunta taʿlamu anna hādha-l-amra [**mention matter in any language]** sharrul-lī fī dīnī wa maʿāshī wa ʿāqibati amrī, faṣrifhu ʿannī waṣrifnī ʿanhu waqdur liya-l-khayra ḥaythu kāna thumma arḍinī bih.

### Stage 6: Look Out For Signs

The signs below have been listed in order of importance. If a higher sign is seen, then take that one and ignore the rest.

For example, if you’re having good
signs in dreams about something, but when you try to do it, it has been made really difficult and
impossible to do, then ignore the dream.

The main sign of a positive Istikharah on an issue is
that the affair will be made easy for you.

#### Good Signs - Go ahead with it!
- The affair made easy (main sign)
- Chest being expanded (feeling good)
- Dream - requires and explanation

#### Bad Signs - DON’T Go ahead with it!
- Task is made impossible to do
- The passion for the decision goes, no inclination towards it anymore
- Something else being made easy for them

> ## **Summary**
> 1. **Answer the 3 questions** (What you’re good at, enjoy, and what the world needs).
> 1. **Set a vision** for where you want to be in 10–20 years.
> 1. **Work backwards** and make a step-by-step game plan.
> 1. **Build the right environment**: Surround yourself with people who are ambitious, values-driven, and will help you grow.
> 1. **Take action** — even small steps build confidence over time.

title: Starting Early
summary: Ever wonder why so many graduates spend months applying and facing rejections before securing a job?
bodyMd:
## A Common Mistake

Ever wonder why so many graduates spend months applying and facing rejections before securing a job?

One of the key reasons is that many students mistakenly wait until their **final year** to explore career options, build a CV, gain essential skills, and apply for jobs.

This delay leads to:

- Missed opportunities

- Lack of application practice

- No industry experience

On the other hand, students who ”S**tart Early”** gain **major advantages **over everyone else.

## **
** Three Advantages of Students Who Start Early

1. More likely to have **gained experience** in industry and obtained key skills

1. More likely to know which **specific field of work** they are interested in

1. Much more **familiar with the job application process**

## Practical Steps: Example Timeline for a 3-Year Degree

### **First Year**

- **Start researching** jobs in industries you're interested in

- **Check for Spring Weeks and Insight Days**

- Create a **basic CV** and set up a **LinkedIn** profile

- **Apply** to Spring Weeks and Insight Days (especially **Sep–Jan**)

### **Second Year**

- Attend **career fairs** and **networking events**

- Refine **CV** and **LinkedIn**; consider finding a **mentor**

- Practice with **mock interviews** and **online assessments**

- **Apply for summer internships** (especially **Aug–Mar**)

### **Third Year**

- Refine everything: **CVs, Cover Letters, LinkedIn, Network, Interview Skills, Assessment Practice**

- Attend **graduate career fairs** and explore job websites

- **Apply for graduate roles and schemes** (especially **Aug–Mar**)

Continue reading the rest of the handbook while thinking about what you can start implementing **early - **especially anything that has deadlines.

title: Building a Personal Brand
summary: Your university years can be hectic; juggling coursework, family, society roles, and the occasional last minute essay panic.
bodyMd:
Your university years can be hectic; juggling coursework, family, society roles, and the occasional *last minute essay panic*.

You might hear people talk about *“LinkedIn”* and *“personal branding.”* But it all sounds distant. Like something people in corporate jobs worried about- not someone like you.

However the truth is that the first place people will search for you professionally is LinkedIn. If you don’t tell your story, someone else will, or worse, no one will.

But first, a crucial point:

## **“Am I Showing Off?” – Navigating Intentions**

As Muslims, we're taught to do things sincerely- not for praise, likes, or recognition. So when it comes to platforms like LinkedIn and building a personal brand, it's natural to ask:

 Is posting about my achievements spiritually damaging self-promotion?

 Am I compromising sincerity by taking credit for work and achievements online?

 Am I at risk of evil eye by having my accolades publicly available?

These are valid questions. And the answer isn’t black and white. It’s about reframing your perspective.

### **Here’s a Balanced Way to Think About It:**

| ***It's not about...*** | ***It's more about...*** |
| --- | --- |
| Seeking Praise | Sharing benefit & growth |
| Boasting | Inspiring & connecting |
| Ego | Encouragement, impact, and visibility for good |

### **Practical Reminders to Stay Grounded**

- **Renew your intention** before posting: Remind that you are sharing this to help others, connect meaningfully, and open doors for a halal income for yourself, not to impress.

- **Stay humble in your tone: **Use language such as **“**I’m grateful for this opportunity” or “I learned a lot from this experience”

- **Stay spiritually protected: **Recite daily adhkar (remembrances)**, e**specially Surah Al-Falaq, Surah An-Naas, and Ayat Al-Kursi to protect yourself from evil eye and remember to say “MashaAllah TabarakAllah” when viewing other peoples achievements.

- **Acknowledge your support systems and be generous with credit. **Mention mentors, teams, or blessings that helped you succeed and most importantly Allah SWT.

> #### **Top Tip: Use Accessible Language for Wider Impact**
> As Muslims, we often use phrases like *Alhamdulillah* or *InshaAllah* in our everyday speech, and naturally, they may appear in our posts too. But not everyone reading will understand their meaning.
> By simply including a short translation, you not only make your message more accessible - you also open a subtle and powerful door to **dawah** (inviting others to understand Islam).
> Your words might be the first time someone sees how faith and gratitude shape a Muslim’s worldview.
> **Here’s how to do it naturally:
> ***“Alhamdulillah (All praise is due to God), I’ve accepted a graduate role in sustainability…”
> “Looking forward to the new year, InshaAllah (God willing).”*
> It takes just a moment but your small effort could leave a lasting impact.

Always remember:

> You are allowed to show up.

If your intention is to grow, uplift others, and represent your community with dignity - that can be an act of ibadah (worship) and dawah (inviting others to Islam).

## **Why LinkedIn Matters (Yes, Even as a Student)**

With **900M+ users worldwide**, LinkedIn is where:

- Careers can begin, grow, and pivot

- You shape your professional identity

- You find people who understand your goals *and* your values

Whether you want to...

- Work at a top firm

- Break into data, design, or marketing

- Build a business

- Or explore purpose-driven careers

**LinkedIn helps you show the world who you are.**

For Muslim students, it’s not just about listing your grades, it's about telling your story, showcasing your values, and building connections who understand where you’re coming from and where you’re going.

## The Benefits

- **Your profile = your personal brand:** Your profile is more than a digital CV. It’s where you show not just what you’ve done, but who you are, what you believe in, and where you want to go.

- **Meaningful Networking**: Finding a mentor who understands both your career goals, your values and your barriers is made possible through LinkedIn

- **Opportunities Can Find *****You***: It’s not an exaggeration. A well written profile means recruiters may actually come to you, without you even applying.

- **Jobs, Internships, & Opportunities**: LinkedIn is a job board, a research tool, and an opportunity finder all in one.

## ** Profile Checklist**

If you are feeling overwhelmed start with this simple recipe

### **1⃣ Profile Picture**

Your photo is the first thing people see. Keep it simple: clear, bright, and modestly professional. Try to avoid mirror selfies and group photos.

### **2⃣ Banner Image**

Think of this as your digital billboard. Use a clean design and clear text such as:

*"Aaliyah | Future Sustainability Consultant | Passionate About Climate Justice"*.

Here are some templates to get started: [Canva LinkedIn Banner Templates](https://www.canva.com/linkedin-banners/templates/)

### **3⃣ Headline**

Avoid just writing: "Student".

Use this space to express your interests and direction, perhaps highlighting past impressive experiences.

For example:

*“Computer Science Student | Ex-Netflix SWE Intern | Interested in Ethical AI & Tech for Good”*

*“Politics & IR Graduate | Passionate About Social Justice & Community Organising”*

### **4⃣ Summary (About Section)**

Your “why,” in your own words.

Include:

- What you're studying

- What drives you

- Projects, roles, or experiences that shaped you

- What you care about

Keep it warm, honest, and purposeful.

For example:

*I am a final year Environmental Science student at the University of Birmingham, with a strong academic foundation and a growing portfolio of experience in sustainability, leadership, and community engagement.*

*My interests lie at the intersection of environmental policy, ethical leadership, and social impact. I have led several initiatives both on campus and within my local community, including coordinating an eco-awareness campaign through the Islamic Society and facilitating workshops for youth focused on environmental responsibility.*

### **5⃣ Experience & Education**

You *don’t* need a fancy internship. You can include (continuing on the previous example):

- Volunteering at your local mosque

- Part time tutoring job

- Leading the Islamic Society’s eco-project

- A virtual internship

- Platforms like [**The Forage**](https://www.theforage.com)**, **[**Coursera**](https://www.coursera.org/courseraplus?utm_medium=sem&utm_source=gg&utm_campaign=b2c_emea_x_coursera_ftcof_courseraplus_cx_dr_bau_gg_sem_bd-ex_gb_en_m_hyb_24-09_x&campaignid=21725850922&adgroupid=351685083790&device=c&keyword=coursera&matchtype=e&network=g&devicemodel=&creativeid=1449957450600&assetgroupid=&targetid=kwd-36262515261&extensionid=&placement=&gad_source=1&gbraid=0AAAAADdKX6YX6-6Tgkw9L80dXDj1BBojg&gclid=Cj0KCQjwna6_BhCbARIsALId2Z2pD1sknfd9oN3WQSWMkhvYxjWCckHZKhf7xLE0-v8N8mM-O9Cb8g4aAlceEALw_wcB)**, **[**Udemy**](https://www.udemy.com/?srsltid=AfmBOopgr_F14b9AScPoMeEKj22J-bIKitnH74GgV-aC8JojUobh-x4E)** **and[** LinkedIn Learning**](https://learning.linkedin.com/cx/get-started?mcid=7198411097454903347&src=go-pa&trk=sem-ga_campid.21301455344_asid.163286450595_crid.699771780927_kw.linkedin%20learning_d.c_tid.kwd-47311766595_n.g_mt.e_geo.9196633&cid=&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gbraid=0AAAAADQDH5RkomjAfyqTSwjKzOM_-PpNx&gclid=Cj0KCQjwna6_BhCbARIsALId2Z3gZQGJ4hvT5NFmYV1X3EYhywDyKIN8b7rU5md4Abx0tPzSCHFMnSYaAlreEALw_wcB)** **(your university may offer this for free)** , **[**SpringPod**](https://www.springpod.com/virtual-work-experience/search)** **offer excellent free courses with certificates you can upload to the ‘certificates’ section.

Tip: Focus on what you *learned and measurably achieved*, not just what your role was.

## ** Growing Your Network (Without It Feeling Awkward)**

Start by connecting with:

- Course mates

- Teachers

- Family

- People you met at events

Then branch out, send messages to people you admire if you have specific question. You would be surprised by the number of people reply. Remember that you miss all the shots you don’t take.

## ** Sharing Your Voice (This is what Makes you Stand Out)**

Don’t just post when you secure internships. You can share:

- Reflections on your industry, perhaps from a faith driven lens

- Thoughts from articles you read

- Lessons from volunteering

- Repost content you found engaging and why

This not only makes your profile engaging, but it also attracts the right people. Mentors, recruiters, and fellow Muslims in your field.

> #### **Quick Tips on Sharing Content**
> - Comment on content you find interesting
> - Share your opinions politely and thoughtfully
> - Write short articles if you enjoy writing
> - Always stay respectful. You are representing yourself, your community, and your values
> - Use hashtags to increase visibility (#STEM, #Marketing, #MuslimProfessionals etc.)

**LinkedIn is not just for professionals. It's for you, the student, the soon to be graduate, the one who has something valuable to offer.** You don’t need to wait until you’ve “made it.” You just need to start.

title: Networking & Career Events

bodyMd:
**Did you know that around 75% of jobs are filled through the hidden job market? (**[**source**](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/careers/jobs-and-experience/finding-jobs-and-internships/)**)**

That means most opportunities are never publicly advertised.

So how do people land these roles? **Through connections**. Whether it’s insider tips, referrals, or being in the right room at the right time - networking can unlock doors you didn’t even know existed.

And even for advertised roles, networking often gives you a serious edge.

***But how do we network with integrity and without feeling fake?***

The answer: **Akhlaq, sincerity, and intention.** Treat networking as a form of *relationship-building for the sake of good*- not self-promotion.

## A Reminder on Akhlaq (Character)

> “…إِنَّ مِنْ أَحَبِّكُمْ إِلَىَّ وَأَقْرَبِكُمْ مِنِّي مَجْلِسًا يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ أَحَاسِنَكُمْ أَخْلاَقًا”

“The most beloved of you to me and the closest to me on the Day of Judgment will be those of you with the best character.”

Every time you reach out to someone, attend an event, or ask for advice - you’re not just representing yourself. You’re representing your values. Your adab (manners) and sincerity will leave a far deeper impression than any polished CV ever could.

> ### Work Smarter Not Harder: Aminah vs Zaynab
> Aminah applies to 50 graduate jobs, tailoring every application and pouring hours into her job search- but hears nothing back.
> Zaynab has a chat with a guest speaker at an event, follows up on LinkedIn, and a few weeks later, lands an internship through that new connection.
> She *never even applied *in the traditional way.
> **Networking doesn’t replace effort - it multiplies your effort. **

Let’s break down **two practical and high-impact ways** to start building connections.

## 1. Coffee Chats

A **coffee chat** is a short, informal conversation with someone working in a field or company you're interested in. It’s **not a job interview** - it’s a chance to learn, gain insights, and build authentic professional relationships.

These chats can give you insider knowledge that makes your future applications more tailored, confident, and strategic.

### Step 1: 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲

Use LinkedIn, professional networks ([check out our directory](/31a9a9520ce481cab84eff7f1e2e1cca?pvs=25)), or event attendee lists.

**Focus on:**

- Alumni from your course or university

- People in roles or companies you're targeting

- Speakers from career panels or events you’ve attended

Try searching:

- “[Company] + [University]” on LinkedIn

- Job titles like “Analyst at PwC” or “Trainee Solicitor at Linklaters”

- Use LinkedIn’s **Alumni Tool** (super underrated)

### Step 2: **Reach Out Effectively**

Send a short, polite message introducing yourself, mentioning what you’re curious about, and asking for a quick 15–20 minute chat.

Don’t worry if not everyone replies - this is normal. Be consistent and respectful. Remember too that people often have busy schedules.

Useful Templates:

- [LinkedIn/ Email Networking Guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1DsS_Wv5MT2ptcGw04fi4P_pT9P4zQS6i90i9FiysTzo/edit?usp=sharing)

- [Reach out docs](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rmKBiY0dmN5uq4iipx3FYHCui1uox3URXcfVEuI7_FA/edit?usp=sharing)

- [Templates- Email](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11lZPSIsQQR7oXmUhqX8L2-mW4dOGzZLQkncvAadlURU/edit?usp=sharing)

- [Templates-LinkedIn](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11ALjtzLyl5t_a9MJy3Zzvu_JJAOFHm8aRiMI3p6QMp8/edit?usp=sharing)

### Step 3: **Have a Meaningful Conversation**

Focus less on impressing them - and more on **learning from them**. People respond well to genuine curiosity and good questions.

> #### Top Tip: Be Present
> Remember to be *interested*, not just *interesting*. You are there to learn so don’t be afraid to ask questions and remember to give people your full attention when talking to them.

Sample questions to ask:

- Could you give me a 2-minute overview of what working in [division] typically involves?

- What aspects of the application process did you find most challenging, or what do you wish you had prepared for differently?

- What do you find most rewarding about your role at XYZ company?

- What are the main challenges that you and your team encounter in your role?

- Would you be willing to connect me with others in this field who might share additional insights?

### Step 4: **Follow Up**

Aim to thank them within 24 hours and highlight something specific you appreciated from the conversation. This small act is often what turns a chat into an ongoing connection and makes it easier to ask for something in the future like a referral.

**Example follow-up lines:**

- “I’ll look into [X resource or advice you gave] and let you know how it goes.”

- “Would it be okay if I check in later this term once I’ve made some progress with [X task]?”

- “Was really nice to connect today! If anyone else comes to mind who I could speak to about [X topic], I’d be grateful for an intro.”

## 2. Career Events & Networking Opportunities

Career events are one of the best places to build multiple connections quickly. These are often advertised on company websites or via your university careers service and provide a perfect opportunity to develop relationships with professionals in your desired industry.

Events include:

- Career fairs

- Employer presentations

- Insight days

- Student conferences

- University alumni meetups

Here are three key steps to help you get the most out of career events (and stand out):

### Step 1: **Have an Elevator Pitch Ready**

This is a 30–60 second intro that covers:

- Who you are (course, year, interests)

- What you’re exploring (career path, sector, company)

- Why you’re interested (genuine curiosity or mission alignment)

#### Example:

> “Hi, I’m Samira, a second year Politics student at LSE. I’ve recently developed an interest in public policy consulting, especially around social impact. I saw you’ve worked in both policy and strategy roles, and I’d love to hear more about how you made that transition.”

### Step 2: **Do Your Homework**

Before the event:

- Look up the attendees or firms in advance

- Have 1–2 thoughtful questions ready for each

- Keep your LinkedIn updated and open to connect

#### Questions you can ask:

- “What kind of candidates thrive in your company’s culture?”

- “How does your team approach mentorship or growth for new grads?”

- “What’s one thing students often overlook when applying to your firm?”

### Step 3: **Build a Relationship After the Event**

After your conversation:

- Send a short thank you message (mention something specific)

- Connect on LinkedIn

- Follow up after applying or acting on their advice

#### Examples of staying in touch:

- “Just wanted to thank you again - I applied to [role] and your advice made a big difference.”

- “I saw your post on [topic] - really insightful, especially the part about [X].”

- “Would love to reconnect in a few weeks after [exam season / application deadline] if you’re open to it.”

## Build, Don’t Just Collect

Networking isn’t about collecting business cards or contacts - it’s about building **authentic relationships** over time.

Here’s how:

- Update them when you take action on their advice

- Congratulate them on career moves or achievements

- Share articles or opportunities related to their interests

- Occasionally ask for further insight or feedback

bodyMd:
A lot of students don’t know how to leverage their university education to help with the career application process.

As important as work experience and everything else is, your actual degree itself can be extremely helpful with career applications.

But only if you know how to make the most of it.

Here are **four key strategies **you need to use to make sure your degree adds the most value to your career journey:

## #1 Create a Coursework Portfolio

> Why it matters: Your projects and coursework can provide powerful material for CVs, LinkedIn, and interviews.

Important: Coursework projects are extremely useful to add on your CV if you do not have any previous work experience, for example, when you apply to your first internships or spring weeks.

### What to Record

- **What you had to do** in the project/task

- **Challenges or problems**, and how they were resolved

- **Results and feedback** you received

### Use It For

- Answering common interview questions like:

### Portfolio Tips

- Save pictures of **physical creations**

- Save **digital work and reports** in organised folders

- Reflect on your experiences for future applications

## #2 Learn Technical Skills

> Use your degree to pick up industry-relevant technical skills that boost employability-even if you're not a tech student. Mention this on your CV or in your interviews.

### STEM Skills

- LaTeX

- CAD software (AutoCAD, SolidWorks)

- Programming languages: Python, MATLAB, C++, R

- Engineering tools: ANSYS, COMSOL

- Machine learning: TensorFlow, scikit-learn

### Humanities & Social Sciences Skills

- Archival research

- Excel, SPSS, Tableau

- Academic writing

- Foreign languages

- Adobe Suite, Canva, InDesign

- GIS tools

- SEO writing, transcription (NVivo, Otter), social media analytics

- Project management tools (Trello, Asana)

- Public speaking & presentation

### Practical Steps

- Take advantage of skill-building modules in your course

- Try software tools even if they're optional

- Add your technical skills to your **CV and LinkedIn profile**

- Get involved in societies and clubs where you can practice

> ### **Switching Fields?**
> You might want to break into a career **not directly tied **to your degree (e.g. Maths → Consulting or Arts → Software Dev). This is absolutely possible-but requires **extra effort **and a demonstrated interest/aptitude in the field outside of your formal education. **Start early** to build and practice the skills you'll need in that industry.

## #3 Boost Your Grades

> Aiming for a 2:1 or First Class keeps more doors open-especially for competitive graduate jobs. Be aware of the fact that many graduate jobs ask for a minimum of a 2:1.

### 5 Practical Strategies to Improve Your Studying

1. Find a study space where you can focus deeply

1. Reduce distractions-limit social media and phone use

1. Prioritise and plan - use early mornings (they have barakah!)

1. Speak to students in the year above for advice and tips

1. Form study groups for difficult topics-two heads are better than one!

## #4 Leverage University Resources

> Why it matters: Your university offers free resources and support that are designed to help you succeed - academically and professionally. Most students either underuse them or don’t know they exist.

Tapping into these services can give you a huge advantage, especially early in your career.

### Careers Service

Most universities have careers centres with:

- **1:1 career guidance sessions**

- **CV, cover letter & application reviews**

- **Mock interviews and assessment centre prep**

- **Career fairs and employer networking events**

- **Access to job boards** and exclusive internship schemes

### Academic Staff & Lecturers

Don’t underestimate the value of **lecturers, tutors, or supervisors**:

- They can provide **personalised references**

- Offer **career advice** within their subject area

- Introduce you to **research opportunities or academic networks**

- May know **former students** in the industry you’re exploring

### Alumni Network

Many universities have:

- **Alumni platforms** where you can search by job title, company, or location

- Guest speakers who are graduates from your degree

### Online Platforms & Tools

Many unis provide free access to costly premium tools:

- **LinkedIn Learning** (technical & soft skills courses)

- **VMock / CV360** for CV feedback

- **Handshake, TargetJobs, Bright Network** for job discovery

- **Vault / GoinGlobal** for industry insights and global career info

### Societies & Student Clubs

Joining student societies is more than just social - it can be strategic:

- Run events or hold positions = **project experience**

- Network with professionals and alumni

- Collaborate across disciplines

- Start initiatives that showcase leadership

One of the best ways to boost your employability and secure a graduate role is through **early exposure to the working world**. Whether it's a Spring Week, Insight Day, or Internship, these experiences help you build key skills, understand industries, and grow your network.

In many cases, doing well during an internship can lead to a **return offer**-a fast-track to a full-time graduate job.

## Key Terms Explained

### **Internships**

Short-term, paid work experiences (usually over summer) normally for students in their **penultimate year** or recent graduates. Internships help you apply what you’ve learned, explore career paths, and gain valuable contacts.

### **Spring Weeks**

1-2 week placements in **March or April** designed for **first-year** students (or second years on a four-year course). These give early insight into sectors like finance, consulting, law, and tech usually being provided exclusively by major firms.

### **Insight Days**

Single-day or short events for students of **any year** (sometimes even sixth formers). They involve talks, networking, and workshops to help you explore different industries and company cultures.

> #### Why It Matters: Zain vs Hasan
> Imagine Zain and Hasan both apply for a graduate software engineering role. Both have great grades and similar backgrounds.
> But Hasan completed an internship last summer. Zain didn’t.
> **All else being equal, Hasan is more likely to get the job-because he has relevant industry experience.** Employers value proven interest and practical skills.

## ** Where can I find Spring Weeks and Internships?**

| Professional networking platform that offers internship listings and networking opportunities. | [**LinkedIn**](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/) |
| Curated list of placements and internships for international students in the UK. | [**Student Circus**](https://studentcircus.com) |
| Advertises internships and work placements across different industries. | [**Internwise**](https://www.internwise.co.uk) |
| Job search platform with company reviews and internship listings. | [**Glassdoor**](https://www.glassdoor.co.uk/index.htm) |

| Connects students with internships and work experience opportunities. | [**Workfinder**](https://www.workfinder.com) |

### In-Person Opportunities

#### **University Careers Service **

Subscribe to their email job alerts. Can contain jobs found nowhere else from companies who want to hire from your specific university.

#### **Careers Fairs**

Great chance to speak directly with recruiters and hear about hidden opportunities. Check out the [networking](/31a9a9520ce4812ba98ef24687c5d4e3?pvs=25) section of this guide on how to best capitalise.

## Tips for Application Questions

If applications involve detailed questions (e.g. motivation, strengths), use the **STAR method **(we go into more detail in the [interviews](/31a9a9520ce48174ab44fb7eb67bb3c0?pvs=25) page):

> **S**ituation What was the context?

> **T**ask – What were you asked to do?

> **R**esult – What was the outcome? Be specific and quantify if you can!

bodyMd:
A CV and cover letter are arguably the most important part of applying to jobs through traditional means. It is at this stage that most candidates get filtered out so It follows that this is a crucial to paint the best image of yourself and your acheivements as possible.

> ### Reminder: Confidence ≠ Arrogance
> You can acknowledge your strengths and achievements without crossing into pride. True confidence is rooted in gratitude, not ego.
> It’s still understandable that when writing a CV and listing your accomplishments you could feel shallow or a degree of self-amazement. All this requires is a shift in mindset. Remind yourself that your achievements have only been accomplished by the will of God and everything goes back to him.

## CV: Your Career Snapshot

Your **CV (Curriculum Vitae)** is a powerful document that summarises your qualifications, experiences, skills, and achievements - all on 1-2 pages. It’s often the first impression an employer will have of you and is arguably the most important component of a traditional job application.

### Key Points

#### Tailor your CV to different jobs

Making your CV match as close as possible to the job description is crucial. Prioritise the **most relevant experiences** for the role. For example, if a university project you did is actually more aligned with the job role than an internship you did, consider listing it above your internship to highlight its relevance.

#### **How to make your CV stand out**

- Use strong **action verbs**: *Led*, *Created*, *Analysed*, *Delivered*

- **Quantify** achievements: *“Increased engagement by 40%”*, *“Managed a team of 6”*

- Use **clean, professional formatting** (avoid colour-heavy, over-designed templates)

- Generative AI tools can help rephrase and optimise your bullet points - be sure to use these as inspiration and as a starting points

#### **What to do if you have no work experience?**

You probably have more experience than you think! Here’s where to look:

**Extracurricular Activities**

- Clubs, societies, and student leadership roles show initiative, teamwork, and communication

- Choose societies that reflect your interests or target sector (e.g. Finance → Investment societies, Consulting → Case Study Clubs)

**Volunteering & Personal Projects**

- Community projects, charity work, or even managing a personal blog or coding portfolio

- Show what you’ve *done* and what *impact* it had

**Online Courses & Certifications**

- Platforms like Coursera, edX, Udemy, or LinkedIn Learning can add depth

- Highlight areas relevant to the job you're aiming for (e.g. Data Analysis, Digital Marketing, Python)

### Practical Steps

#### **Step 1: Get familiar with high quality examples**

[Imperial College CV & Cover Letters Guide](https://issuu.com/imperialcareers/docs/cv_cover_letter_2024_web?fr=xKAE9_zU1NQ) (shows a CV without much work experience)

[Auralyze AI CV Template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IafqesFpIPXXRpPg6lWMp3xq5G4CfGIS2lOpiRRjYcM/edit?tab=t.0)

[CV Information | Oxford University](https://www.careers.ox.ac.uk/cvs#collapse1542131)

Do your own industry specific research in addition e.g. Search “Successful [X firm] [Y role] CV example”

#### **Step 2: Choose a strong, clean template**

For most industries a Word template is typical. More technical fields such as Computer Science and Software Engineering LaTeX is used.

[Example CV Template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HMKQ5B3vsb4T67Iq7RPBUG68r9E5Wl2c/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=101547915182389275514&rtpof=true&sd=true) (Word format)

[CV Templates](https://www.overleaf.com/gallery/tagged/cv/page/2) (LaTeX format)

#### **Step 3:** **Write in the XYZ format**

**Accomplished [X], as measured by [Y], by doing [Z]**

*Example: “Won second place out of 50 teams in hackathon at Imperial working with two colleagues to develop an app that synchronizes mobile calendars.”*

The reason for this is simple. Vague phrases like “improved efficiency” are subjective and hard to measure. Concrete and tangible figures give anyone who reads your CV a point of reference.

#### **Step 4:** Use Bullet Points and Tailor Wording to the Job Description

They increase readability and make your achievements easier to scan - especially for ATS systems (AI programs used at large companies for an initial screening to scan for keywords).

**What keywords to look for in the job description and include:**

- **Hard Skills & Tools - **e.g. Excel, Python, SQL, Salesforce, Adobe Creative Suite, Power BI

- **Soft Skills - **e.g. Communication, Leadership, Analytical Thinking, Time Management

- **Industry Jargon **- e.g. “Client-facing”, “Agile”, “Stakeholder engagement”, “UX”, “Financial modelling”

- **Qualifications **- e.g. “STEM background”, “Data-driven decision making”, “Lean Six Sigma”, “Audit readiness”

Include them **naturally** where possible in your bullet points or skills sections.

[Free ATS checker](https://enhancv.com/resources/resume-checker/) - use to check the readability of your CV by computers and provides a score, sometimes you can also upload the job description to tailor feedback.

#### **Step 5: Get Multiple Perspectives**

It’s completely normal to not get your CV right on the first go. In fact, it’s **expected**. What sets strong applicants apart is their willingness to **seek feedback** and iterate. Here are people you should take advice from starting with the most impactful:

- **Industry Professionals**

- **Students 1–2 Years Ahead**

- **University Careers Services**

- **Friends, Mentors & Society Members**

You should ideally have revised your CV at least a few times and ran it by multiple people before you start applying to openings.

## Cover Letter

**Your cover letter is your story - make it count.**

A great cover letter isn’t just a repeat of your CV. It’s your chance to show **who you are**, **why you care**, and **why you’re a perfect fit** for the role. Think of it as your personal pitch.

**Research with fake job applications shows that applications with tailored cover letters yield just over 50% more interviews compared to those without. (**[**source**](https://www.resumego.net/research/cover-letters/#:~:text=New%20research%20finds%20that%20applications,to%20each%20individual%20job%20opening%3F)**)**

### Key Points

**A cover letter should be:**

- A short, compelling note to the employer, no longer than one page of A4

- A way to connect your experience to the job

- A chance to show your personality and motivation

- Written clearly and succinctly to highlight the most relevant skills

### Cover Letter Structure

Here's a breakdown you can follow (but add your own flavor):

#### **1. Greeting**

Keep it direct. Use the hiring manager’s name if you can.

> Example: “Dear Ms. Patel, Dear Sir/Madam”

#### **2. Opening Paragraph**

Hook them in! Clearly mention what role you’re applying for and **why** you’re excited about it.

> “I’m thrilled to apply for the Marketing Intern position at X Company because…”

> #### **Pro Tip: Mention Employees You’ve Connected With**
> If you’ve spoken with someone at the company - whether at a career fair, networking event, or through a coffee chat - **include at the start of your cover letter**. It shows **initiative**, **real interest**, and that you’ve done more than just read the job posting.
> “After speaking with [Employee’s Name] at [Event/Platform], I gained valuable insight into [Company Name]’s culture and the [Role Title]. Our conversation confirmed my excitement about this opportunity and how I could contribute to your team.”
> This works because:
> - It makes your letter personal and specific
> - Shows you’ve taken the time to engage
> - Can build credibility if the person you spoke with is respected in the company

#### **3. Middle Paragraph(s)**

This is where you shine.

- Highlight one or two key experiences

- Connect your skills to what the company needs

- Show you’ve done your research on the company and their values

#### **4. Closing Paragraph**

Reaffirm your interest. End with a confident, polite call to action.

> “I’d love to bring my creativity and energy to your team - thank you for the consideration”

#### **5. Signature**

Stick with:

> “Sincerely,” or “Best regards,”

See how it is all put together in this [Cover Letter Template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ec6_2k1wRcOyB6C8BDbDQiTZJb-p2wDvkCRfXEvUWMk/edit?usp=sharing)

title: Mastering Online Tests
summary: With the rise of job applications through the internet, increasingly employers are looking towards online assessments to act as another metric to measure candidates.
bodyMd:
With the rise of job applications through the internet, increasingly employers are looking towards online assessments to act as another metric to measure candidates.

## What Are Online Assessments?

Depending on the role or company, you might face:

- **Situational Judgement Tests (SJTs)** – How would you respond in a tricky work situation?

- **Numerical Reasoning** – Can you interpret data under pressure?

- **Verbal Reasoning** – Can you quickly understand written information?

- **Diagrammatic/Logical Reasoning** – Can you spot patterns and think critically?

- **Gamified Tests** – Think mini-games designed to measure attention, memory, and personality traits.

## Why Do Employers Use Them?

Because they’re:

- **Fast** – Quickly filter large applicant pools

- **Objective** – Score-based, reducing unconscious bias

- **Gatekeepers** – If you don’t hit the score, you may be **auto-rejected** before anyone even reads your application

You could be out before your CV ever gets opened.

## What It Means For You

If you *do well*, these assessments can actually:

- Push you to the **top of the pile**

- Secure you an **interview** (even if your CV isn’t perfect)

> In ultra-competitive roles, “average” isn’t enough - many employers only progress candidates in the top percentile of scorers.

## “No Preparation Needed”?

Some companies *say* you don’t need to prep. But the reality?

Preparation = Advantage

Especially if:

- You’ve noticed you’re not getting past the test stage

- You haven’t taken one before

- You’re applying to a **highly competitive** role or company

## Practical Ways to Prepare for Online Assessments

### ** Research the Assessment Provider:**

Many companies outsource their online assessments to third-party providers (e.g., Arctic Shores). If you can identify the assessment provider (try a quick search on Google, YouTube, or by asking others who have taken the test) it can give you valuable insight into the question style and what to expect.

### ** Align Your Answers with Company Values**

Carefully review the job description and familiarise yourself with the company’s core values. Tailor your responses, particularly in situational judgement questions, to reflect these values.

For example, if the company places a strong emphasis on integrity, ensure your answers demonstrate honesty and ethical decision-making.

### ** Make Use of Practice Assessments**

Use the online practice assessments to get really good at these tests. Practising online assessments can significantly improve your performance.

Here is a range of online resources designed to help you master these tests.

Note: Your university will often pay for practice tests so do make sure to check with careers service

**Disclaimer: **The provided descriptions may not be fully accurate at the time you visit.

So you’re at the interview stage, well done! That means the company already sees potential in you to some extent. You just need to convey your passion, aptitude and capabilities for the job during the interview.

## Understanding the Interview Landscape

It important to know what type of interview you are facing and what to expect. You can do this by:

- **Checking the job description** (sometimes it’s listed)

- **Checking the interview confirmation email**

- **Emailing HR or the recruiter**

Interviews come in different forms, here are a couple:

- **Behavioural:** To assess how you handled real-life situations in the past. (Tell me about a time...)

- **Technical: **To test your role-specific knowledge or hands-on ability. (Coding tests, portfolio reviews)

- **Situational: **To assess your approach to hypothetical work scenarios. (What would you do if...)

- **Case Studies / Estimation:** To assess your business and strategy toolkit. (Most common in consulting)

- **Group / Panel Interviews: **To observe how you interact in team settings or with multiple decision-makers.

## ** Preparation**

### Research the Company

Look into:

- The company’s **mission & values**

- Their **workplace culture** (LinkedIn posts, Glassdoor, team bios)

- **Recent news, projects, or updates** to reference in your conversation

- Your interviewer (normally they tell you who this is in your invite email)

### **Practice Common Questions**

- For behavioural questions have stories and anecdotes from your experiences to talk about in different situations. Use the **STAR(R) Method:**

- Have answers ready to common general questions like:

> ### Pre-Interview Dua
> When Musa (AS) was commanded by Allah SWT to confront Pharaoh, he was understandably anxious. He worried about his speech and his ability to convey the message effectively. In response to this daunting task, he made a beautiful dua
> قَالَ رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى وَيَسِّرْ لِىٓ أَمْرِى وَٱحْلُلْ عُقْدَةًۭ مِّن لِّسَانِى يَفْقَهُوا۟ قَوْلِى
> Moses prayed, “My Lord! Uplift my heart for me, and make my task easy, and remove the impediment from my tongue so people may understand my speech
> (Ta-Ha 20:25-28)
> **Reciter: Al-Saut Al-Baki Al-Shaykh Muhammad Siddiq Al-Minshawi**
> This dua is especially relevant for interviews because it asks Allah SWT to grant clarity of thought, ease in tasks, and eloquence in speech. When reciting this dua before an interview, you are essentially seeking Allah’s help to express yourself clearly and effectively.

## ** Making a Solid First Impression**

The first ten seconds of meeting your interviewer a critical deciding factor for whether you will be hired or not.

### Remote Interviews (Zoom, Google Meet, etc.)

#### **Setup**

- Find a quiet, well-lit space with a plain background

- Use headphones or earbuds for clear audio

- Sit at a desk or table, not on your bed

- Elevate your laptop to eye level (books work!)

#### Camera and Body Language

- Keep your camera *on* unless otherwise requested

- Sit up straight, smile, and look into the webcam (not the screen)

- Use your hands naturally when speaking - even virtually, it shows energy!

### In-Person Interviews

#### **Logistics Are Key**

- Plan your route and leave buffer time (plan to be 15 mins early)

- Bring a copy of your CV/resume, a notebook, and a pen

- Greet the receptionist and everyone else you interact with professionally - they may give feedback

#### **Presence & Poise**

- Greet with confidence (smile, handshake or polite nod)

- Make good eye contact (as culturally appropriate)

- Pay attention to posture and body language

#### **How do I manage handshakes with the opposite gender?**

## ** Asking good questions**

Asking smart, well-timed questions isn’t just a formality -it’s a **powerful way to show curiosity, preparation, and genuine interest** in the role and the company.

When you ask good questions, you’re telling the interviewer:

> “I care about doing well here, and I’m thinking long-term.”

You can ask questions about:

- **The Role:** “What does a typical day in this role look like?”

- **The Company/Team:** “I saw your team recently launched [project or initiative] - how was that experience?”

- **Development: **“What does progression typically look like in this role or team?”

- **Next Steps: **“What are the next stages in the interview process?”

Remember to not ask questions that have already been answered since it may show that you weren't listening.

## Bonus Tip: Current Events

title: Crushing Assessment Centres
summary: Think of it as the final boss battle in the job hunt - a high-stakes stage where employers get to see you in action. Unlike traditional interviews, assessment centres are immersive, multi-part selection processes designe
bodyMd:
Think of it as the **final boss battle** in the job hunt - a high-stakes stage where employers get to see you in action. Unlike traditional interviews, assessment centres are **immersive, multi-part selection processes** designed to test how you *think*, *communicate*, and *collaborate* under pressure.

You’re not just being assessed on what you know, but **how you operate in real-time**. This is done through:

- Group exercises

- Case studies or problem-solving tasks

- One-on-one or panel interviews

- Presentations (with limited prep time)

- In-tray or e-tray simulations

- Role plays or business scenarios

- Informal networking events (yes — these *count*, too)

Most assessment centres last anywhere from **half a day to two full days**, and by the time you’re invited, it means the employer already sees strong potential in you. Now it’s time to **show up and seal the deal**.

## What Employers Are *Really* Looking For

Spoiler: It’s *not* perfection. Nobody expects you to be flawless or have all the answers. What they’re actually assessing is:

- How you think through problems

- How you behave around others

- How clearly you communicate your ideas

- How well you balance leadership with collaboration

- How you perform under pressure

It’s a test of **potential** - not just polish. They want to see how you show up when things aren’t scripted.

## Prepping Like a Pro

### Understand the Company & Role

- Know their mission, values, current challenges and recent news

- Understand the role’s responsibilities and what competencies they care about most (refer to the job description)

- Learn their competitors, market, and tone - culture fit *does* matter, especially at competitive firms

### Reflect & Rehearse

Use the **STAR method** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to prepare strong stories around:

- Leading a team

- Handling failure

- Solving problems

- Resolving conflict

- Influencing others

- Working under time pressure

### Practice Typical Tasks

Prep platforms like **AssessmentDay**, **JobTestPrep**, or **YouTube videos** can help you simulate:

- Group discussions

- Case studies

- Psychometric or aptitude tests

- Time-bound presentations

- In-tray/e-tray scenarios

Also: sleep well, eat well, stay hydrated. Basic, yes - but crucial for mental performance and sharpness.

## Group Exercises: Play the Social Game Strategically

Group tasks are there to test **collaboration, communication, and leadership** — not dominance.

#### How to shine:

- Actively listen and build on others’ ideas

- Encourage quieter voices: “Sarah, what’s your take on this?”

- Offer to structure the task or keep time: “Let’s keep track so we stay focused.”

- Summarise what’s been discussed to move things forward: “So far, it sounds like we’re leaning toward…”

#### What to avoid:

- Talking over others or dominating the task

- Sticking to just one role (e.g., only being the timekeeper)

- Getting flustered when the task gets messy — that’s *part* of the challenge

**Pro tip**: Be the person who helps the group move — not just speak.

## Interviews: Behavioural & Strength-Based

You’ll likely face one (or more) interviews. These could be **competency-based**, **strength-based**, or a mix of both.

### Competency Questions:

Prepare those STAR stories!

- “Tell me about a time you handled a difficult team member.”

- “Describe a time you worked under pressure.”

- “Give an example of when you led a project successfully.”

### Strength-Based Questions:

Focus on energy, not just experience.

- “What comes naturally to you?”

- “What tasks energise you the most?”

- “When do you feel most productive?”

Be honest. These are designed to uncover your *fit* and what motivates you.

## Case Studies & Presentations: Thinking on Your Feet

You’ll be given a business scenario and a short window to:

- Analyse the info

- Form a recommendation

- Present your solution (often solo, sometimes in a group)

### How to approach it:

1. **Scan** quickly for key numbers, trends, or goals

1. **Prioritise** issues - don’t try to fix everything

1. **Structure clearly**:

Speak confidently - even if you’re unsure. You’re being assessed on how you **structure and communicate**, not just the final answer.

## In-Tray & E-Tray: Simulate the Job

You’ll handle realistic emails, reports, and memos - prioritising tasks, responding to requests, or flagging issues.

#### What to show:

- Time management and decision-making

- Logic in prioritisation (urgency vs. importance)

- Professional written tone

- Clarity in reasoning

**Tip**: Imagine yourself already in the role. What would your manager expect?

## Informal Events: Still Under the Microscope

Chatting with candidates or recruiters over lunch? Small talk during breaks?

These moments are still part of the assessment. They give insights into your **professionalism, curiosity, and interpersonal skills**.

- Ask thoughtful questions

- Show genuine interest in others

- Be polite, relaxed, and present

## Staying Calm is the Secret Weapon

Assessment centres are designed to **test your limits**, but they’re not meant to break you. If something doesn’t go perfectly, **let it go and move on** - there are multiple chances to impress.

- Focus on each task, one at a time

- Be flexible and self-aware

- Don’t fake it - show up as a **switched-on version of yourself**

- Remember: they’re hiring for potential, not perfection

title: Dealing With Rejection
summary: Being rejected - not just once, but multiple times - is part of the process for most people. Even if you’ve studied at a top university or done everything “right,” the path to landing job offers is rarely smooth.
bodyMd:
Being rejected - **not just once, but multiple times - **is part of the process for most people. Even if you’ve studied at a top university or done everything “right,” the path to landing job offers is rarely smooth.

Even once you are within a job and looking to get onto certain projects, get promoted or switch firms rejection is inevitable.

This can take a **real emotional toll**, especially when rejections pile up. That’s why it’s essential to have strategies in place to **process rejection**, build resilience, and keep moving forward-with clarity, confidence, and tawakkul (trust in Allah).

## The Impacts of Rejection

Rejection doesn’t just sting - it can affect your mindset and motivation. Here are some common emotional responses to be aware of:

### **#1 Rumination**

*Replaying the event again and again in your head, asking “what if…”*

### **#2 Performance Pressure**

*Feeling like there’s more pressure than ever to succeed next time*

### **#3 Reduced Energy & Motivation**

*Feeling drained, disheartened, or unsure whether to keep trying*

### **#4 Hopelessness**

*Starting to believe that no matter what you do, things won’t improve*

## Mentally Preparing Early (Before Applying)

Set your mindset before the applications begin:

- **Detach from the outcome**

- **Your Rizq (provision) is already written**

## Emotional Management After Rejection

### How do I deal with **rumination**?

- **Change your perspective**: Imagine you're giving advice to a friend-what would you say to *them*?

- **Shift your focus**: Go for a walk, play a sport, or do something creative. Give your mind something else to chew on.

### How do I deal with **sadness and hopelessness**?

- **Gratitude journaling**: Write down your blessings and past wins-even small ones. Remind yourself of your growth.

- **Look around**: Reflect on those who may be struggling with less than you have. It helps reset your perspective.

### How do I **move on**?

- **Review and reflect**: Ask the company for feedback, most are happy to provide it unless stated otherwise. Was there a lesson in this? Did you miss anything useful - like interview tips or CV tweaks?

- **Take a short break**: Sometimes, a little space helps recharge your motivation.

- **Re-approach with renewed energy**: You’re wiser than before. Each rejection is just a redirection.

title: Navigating Workplace Barriers
summary: Being a minority group in the UK and Ireland means that there are a few things to think about when navigating the workplace.
bodyMd:
Being a minority group in the UK and Ireland means that there are a few things to think about when navigating the workplace.

## Set Clear Boundaries

- Don’t shy away from sharing your religious needs - the sooner you do this the earlier you set a precedent.

- Block out **Jumu’ah** and **prayer times** on your calendar.

- Be open about **fasting during Ramadan**, your **dietary needs**, or avoiding alcohol-related events.

- Be polite, firm, and professional-people respect clarity and good manners (akhlaq).

## Protect Your Salah

- Enquire if your office space or a nearby one has prayer facilities.

- If not available, use meeting rooms, multifaith spaces, quiet corners-even parks.

- In all cases when performing ablution or praying be sure to respect facilities and aim to leave it better than you found it.

> ### Reminder: Virtue of Salah
> Salah is non-negotiable-it anchors your day and reminds you of your ultimate purpose of worshipping God
> **وَٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَلَىٰ صَلَاتِهِمْ يُحَافِظُون
> أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ فِى جَنَّـٰتٍۢ مُّكْرَمُونَ **
> **-Reciter: Al-Saut Al-Baki Al-Shaykh Muhammad Siddiq Al-Minshawi
> **Remember that God is Al-Sami (All-Hearing), Al-Basir (All-Seeing). No efforts you make to maintain your daily prayers, no matter how small, will be missed.

## Handle Social Norms with Grace

- Avoid awkward handshake moments with a kind smile and a hand over the heart.

- Alcohol at work events? Suggest alternatives: halal lunch spots, coffee catchups, or fun group activities. Another option is to join for food or early networking, then head out.

## Navigating Value Clashes

- Stay calm when faced with differing views (e.g., LGBTQ topics, Palestine). Remember you don’t need to engage with every topic of discussion.

- Know your rights-**you’re not required to express views** that conflict with your faith as it is a protected characteristic under law.

- Be respectful, professional, and clear on your values. Remind yourself of your intentions and the reason you are there.

## Find Other Muslims at Work

- Look out for fellow Muslims-it’s easier when you’re not alone.

- You might meet them during prayer breaks, Ramadan chats, or through employee networks.

- Create a group chat, organise prayer together, or start a faith-based network if one doesn’t exist.

- Being coordinated gives you strength in numbers when asking for facilities and accommodations.

title: Being an Ambassador for Islam
